option: AWS
summary: boto3/Terraform aws; most common recruiter keyword

option: Decide per project
summary: cloud-agnostic scaffold, choose at plan time

option: Files only, no MCP
summary: markdown/JSON + skills; nothing enforces the rules

option: Docker stack like ai-task-factory
summary: Postgres + API + HTTP MCP; far more to build and run

option: Public repo now
summary: visible portfolio immediately

option: One public repo per project, each with its own plane; factory repo private and packaged as a plugin
rationale: The only split that keeps stf's evidence checks working, and it answers the portfolio-visibility question in OQ-003.
summary: Each of devsecops-pipeline, hardened-iac, malware-sandbox and zero-trust-audit gets its own GitHub repo, public from the first commit, holding the code, specs/, .stf/export/ and project rules. secops-task-factory stays private and ships tools/stf-mcp, skills and hooks as a Claude Code plugin.
tradeoffs: Pro: public history per project; evidence stays verifiable because the code and the plane that hashes it share one git root; GitHub-to-Azure OIDC trust is scoped to one repo. Con: five setups; no shared recall or memory across projects; plugin versions to keep in step; spec numbering restarts per repo unless charter takes an explicit seq.

option: Keep one private monorepo (factory + projects under projects/)
rationale: The portfolio goal needs projects that are visible, and splitting later would break recorded evidence.
summary: The status quo from D-003: everything lives in the private secops-task-factory repo.
tradeoffs: Pro: one setup, one recall block across all four specs, shared memory, nothing to migrate. Con: recruiters can't see any project; GitHub code scanning on a private repo needs GitHub Advanced Security (spec 001 Assumptions); CI and OIDC trust span every project.

option: Central factory repo whose plane tracks code in external project repos
rationale: It defeats the evidence guarantees the factory exists for, unless stf gains multi-root support, which is out of scope.
summary: Keep specs/ and .stf/export/ in secops-task-factory, and put only the code in per-project repos.
tradeoffs: Pro: one recall block and one memory. Con: the server refuses artefact paths outside its repo root (repoRelative), and checks commits and history only in its own repo (commitExists, inGitHistory). Outcome capture and checkpoints would be refused, and verify would report absent.

option: Build in the private monorepo, then mirror each project to a public repo at milestones
rationale: The public copy would lose exactly the verifiable evidence that makes it worth showing.
summary: Periodic git subtree split or filter-repo of projects/<name> into a public repo.
tradeoffs: Pro: work in progress stays hidden, with a single workspace. Con: extraction rewrites commit shas and moves paths, so the public copy can't verify any recorded checkpoint or artefact hash; two histories drift apart.

option: Project repos private until their spec is done, then public
summary: Split now, but only flip visibility once each project is complete.
tradeoffs: Pro: unfinished work stays hidden. Con: code scanning needs GitHub Advanced Security or the run-artefact fallback while the repo is private; no visible progress for recruiters.

option: Make the factory repo public as well
rationale: Operator chose to keep the factory private (2026-09-24). This can be revisited after the roadmap's P0 items land.
summary: Show secops-task-factory itself as a portfolio piece.
tradeoffs: Pro: shows the method as well as the projects. Con: reviewers would probe the known trust gaps (session gate bound to the process, self-reported analyze score) before they are closed.

option: AI embeddings / vector search for memory and recall
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): local full-text memory is enough as long as it works across sessions.
summary: Embed memories and plane records and retrieve them by semantic similarity.
tradeoffs: Pro: fuzzy recall across wording. Con: an embedding model and a vector index to host or call, results that can't be reproduced byte-for-byte, and a new place for secrets to leak.

option: Azure-hosted plane with authentication
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): the plane stays local; no hosted plane, no auth.
summary: Run the plane as a hosted service (API + database) that every repo and session talks to over the network.
tradeoffs: Pro: one live view across machines. Con: infrastructure, cost and an auth surface to secure; state stops travelling with git, so evidence is no longer verifiable from a checkout.

option: Server-side auto-fix of detected problems
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): detection stays verify + analyze gate + refusals; automation goes through /loop or scheduled agents, tracked changes through change requests.
summary: Let the stf server repair what verify or analyze finds (e.g. rewrite files, flip statuses back, regenerate artefacts) on its own.
tradeoffs: Pro: fewer manual steps. Con: the server would change content nobody reviewed, which undoes the point of refusals and hashed evidence.

option: Read the plane only as JSON (stf status / make status)
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25) asked for a simple read-only dashboard instead of reading JSON (Roadmap P1-7).
summary: No HTML view: people read stf_status output or the committed .stf/export/*.json.
tradeoffs: Pro: nothing extra to build. Con: hard to scan phases, tasks, questions and handoffs at a glance.

option: A copy of the status-page scripts in every project repo
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): move it into the plugin so every project repo gets it and keeps only its own pages.json.
summary: Each project repo keeps its own scripts/status-pages (renderers, templates, hook.py) and a project PostToolUse hook, as devsecops-pipeline did first.
tradeoffs: Pro: no plugin change. Con: N copies drift apart, each fix is repeated per repo, and the hook has to locate the plugin's CLI in the plugin cache.

option: Keep the Python renderers (python-markdown via uv)
rationale: Operator preferred CLI verbs next to stf dashboard with no Python/uv dependency; ported to TypeScript with marked, anchors and links verified identical on spec 001.
summary: Ship render_spec.py / render_hub.py inside the plugin and call them through uv.
tradeoffs: Pro: no port. Con: every machine needs Python and uv next to Node; two languages in the plugin.

option: Record a decision only; no moved state in the plane
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25) chose a real moved state that blocks new writes and shows where the spec went.
summary: Note the move in a decision and leave the old spec rows as they are.
tradeoffs: Pro: no code change. Con: status and recall keep showing the old spec as live work at clarify, with its open questions, and nothing stops a session from writing to it.

option: Delete the moved specs' records from the factory plane
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): keep the spec's history intact (questions, decisions, events); only block new writes.
summary: Remove the spec row and its questions, decisions and events once the spec lives elsewhere.
tradeoffs: Pro: a clean plane. Con: loses the history of why things were decided; the plane is meant to be append-only in spirit.

option: Mark all four specs as moved now
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): mark 002–004 later, when they actually move.
summary: Apply the moved state to 001–004 immediately, using planned repo names for 002–004.
tradeoffs: Pro: one step. Con: 002–004 have no repos or planes yet, so the recorded target would point at nothing.

option: Copy the project scaffold by hand for each new repo
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25) asked for a stf new-project skill.
summary: Start each project by copying devsecops-pipeline's first commit (a8ece62) and editing it.
tradeoffs: Pro: nothing to build. Con: error-prone (hook mode, pinned versions, placeholders), and fixes to the scaffold never reach the next project.

option: Charter spec 001 in the new repo's first session
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25): charter during setup, so the new repo starts at specify.
summary: new-project writes files and an empty plane only; the first session in the new repo charters the spec.
tradeoffs: Pro: the scaffold stays minimal. Con: one more manual step before the lifecycle can start.

option: Drop the factory repo's plane once 002–004 have moved
rationale: Operator (2026-09-25) chose to keep the factory plane for factory-level work.
summary: Treat secops-task-factory as tooling only and delete .stf/export.
tradeoffs: Pro: one less thing to maintain. Con: loses the only record of factory-wide decisions, recall in factory sessions, the moved specs' history, and CI's round-trip and verify checks against a real plane.
